argue-by-contradiction.conclusion: Assume not-P. Use the assumed structure to build or derive objects, then show these objects violate a known fact. The contradiction forces P.
argue-by-contradiction.however: Proofs by contradiction can obscure the constructive content of a result, making it harder to extract algorithms or explicit witnesses. Some mathematical communities prefer direct proofs when available.
argue-by-contradiction.title: Argue by Contradiction

check-the-extreme-cases.conclusion: Instantiate the statement at every extreme: n=0, n=1, the empty set, the one-point space, the trivial group, infinite dimension, the identity morphism. Check whether the statement is true, vacuously true, or false. A failure at an extreme case is a cheap disproof.
check-the-extreme-cases.however: Extreme cases can be vacuously true or pathologically special, giving false confidence. Passing extreme-case checks is necessary but not sufficient.
check-the-extreme-cases.title: Check the Extreme Cases

complexity-classification.conclusion: 1. Construct the reduction (typically polynomial-time many-one or Turing) from a complexity-class-complete problem to P (for hardness) or from P to a problem already in C (for membership). 2. Verify the reduction is correct and within the resource bounds for the target class. 3. State the classification theorem: P is C-complete (or C-hard, or in C, as appropriate).
complexity-classification.however: Complexity-classification is *one specific subtype* of `characterization-result` — its analogue in non-computational settings is `classification-result` (e.g., classifying KMS states or AFD outer actions). The reasoning shape is "list-the-cases-and-show-exhaustion" but the deliverable is "the problem belongs to class C" rather than "the structure has these instances." Use this leaf only when the result is genuinely complexity-theoretic.
complexity-classification.title: Complexity Classification

construct-an-explicit-witness.conclusion: Build the object step by step. Define it concretely. Verify each required property. If the construction is complex, build intermediate objects and compose them.
construct-an-explicit-witness.however: Explicit constructions can be intricate and may obscure *why* the object exists. Sometimes a non-constructive proof reveals more about the landscape than a single explicit example.
construct-an-explicit-witness.title: Construct an Explicit Witness

construct-auxiliary-object.conclusion: Identify the gap. Ask: what kind of object would connect my hypothesis to my conclusion? Construct it explicitly. Verify it has the properties needed on both sides. Common auxiliary objects include: truncated random variables, bump functions, test morphisms, approximating sequences, and free resolutions.
construct-auxiliary-object.however: Auxiliary objects can feel like magic when encountered for the first time. The skill is in recognising which construction is needed: truncation, mollification, partition of unity, Hahn-Banach extension, free object on generators, approximating sequence.
construct-auxiliary-object.title: Construct an Auxiliary Object

count-over-a-decomposition.conclusion: Choose the decomposition that isolates the term you want (the center as the singleton classes; the fixed points as the size-1 orbits). Establish the uniform constraint on the other parts. Subtract / take congruences to force the distinguished term.
count-over-a-decomposition.however: The decomposition must be **exhaustive and disjoint** (no part double-counted, none missed), and the shared constraint must genuinely hold on *every* part you are not solving for — one uncounted orbit or one exception breaks the conclusion.
count-over-a-decomposition.title: Count over a Decomposition

dualise-the-problem.conclusion: Reformulate the problem in the dual setting. Solve it there if easier. Translate the solution back. For logical statements, try the contrapositive before attempting direct proof.
dualise-the-problem.however: Not every problem dualises cleanly. Some dualities lose structure (the double dual may not be isomorphic to the original). You must verify that the dual problem actually helps.
dualise-the-problem.title: Dualise the Problem

encode-as-algebra.conclusion: Assign algebraic objects to your problem's ingredients: groups to symmetries, rings to coordinate systems, modules to representations, homology groups to topological spaces. Reformulate the problem as an algebraic question. Solve using algebraic tools (exact sequences, spectral sequences, Groebner bases, character theory).
encode-as-algebra.however: The algebraic translation may lose geometric or combinatorial information. The algebra may be harder to compute with than the original objects. Not every problem benefits from algebraisation.
encode-as-algebra.title: Encode as Algebra

epsilon-of-room.conclusion: Fix an arbitrary ε > 0. Cash in the ε–δ budget from the relevant definition to prove the slack statement. Since ε was arbitrary, take ε → 0 (or inf over ε) to collapse the slack and conclude the sharp statement.
epsilon-of-room.however: The relaxed bound must hold for *all* ε > 0 with the slack genuinely controlled by ε (the bound's right side must tend to the target as ε → 0), and the quantity must live where "≤ ε for every ε > 0 ⇒ ≤ 0" is valid. Watch that any δ, cover, or index chosen to meet one ε does not secretly depend on the thing you are bounding.
epsilon-of-room.title: Give Yourself an Epsilon of Room

estimate-by-bounding.conclusion: Identify which direction you need (upper or lower). Apply the most appropriate standard inequality. Check that the resulting bound is tight enough for your purposes. If not, try a different inequality or a more refined decomposition before bounding.
estimate-by-bounding.however: Bounds lose information. A bound that is too loose is useless. The art is in choosing the tightest bound that remains tractable. Chaining too many inequalities can accumulate slack to the point of triviality.
estimate-by-bounding.title: Estimate by Bounding

exhaustion-as-theorem.conclusion: 1. Identify the common quantitative step where all techniques fail. 2. Formulate the barrier as a theorem: "any technique in class C that proceeds via step X produces a bound of at most f(n)" where f(n) is weaker than the target. 3. Prove the ceiling theorem (often by exhibiting a worst case for step X). 4. Record the ceiling as a lemma. It eliminates the technique class and redirects effort toward techniques outside the class.
exhaustion-as-theorem.however: Consistent failure might be coincidence rather than structure. Before declaring the barrier fundamental, verify that the techniques genuinely span the family — not just three variants of the same idea. Also check whether a technique outside the family avoids the barrier entirely.
exhaustion-as-theorem.title: Exhaustion as Theorem

exploit-symmetry.conclusion: Identify the symmetry group. Use it to reduce to a canonical representative ("without loss of generality"). Count orbits instead of elements. Decompose representations into irreducibles. Apply fixed-point theorems when the action has no escape.
exploit-symmetry.however: Not all apparent symmetries are real: a function may look symmetric but have hidden asymmetries. And exploiting symmetry requires proving the symmetry exists, which itself may be non-trivial.
exploit-symmetry.title: Exploit Symmetry

failure-mode-characterization.conclusion: 1. Construct an explicit counterexample or family of counterexamples that lie just outside H. 2. Identify the structural feature of the counterexamples that makes T fail — the "failure mechanism." 3. State the boundary as a theorem: "T fails iff [structural condition]." 4. Optional: re-prove T with a refined hypothesis H' that excludes the failure regime.
failure-mode-characterization.however: Failure-mode characterization is structurally distinct from a *negative result* (T is false in this case). A negative result asserts something doesn't hold; failure-mode-characterization specifies the *regime* where it doesn't hold and the *structural reason* it doesn't. The latter is stronger — it tells the reader where the theorem still works, where it fails, and *why*.
failure-mode-characterization.title: Failure-Mode Characterization

find-the-right-abstraction.conclusion: Identify the minimal structural assumptions your argument actually uses. Reformulate in terms of those assumptions alone. If a known framework (group, category, topological space, measure space) fits, use it; if not, you may have discovered a new one.
find-the-right-abstraction.however: Premature abstraction obscures rather than clarifies: abstracting before you have enough examples risks building a framework that fits nothing well. The right abstraction is found, not prescribed.
find-the-right-abstraction.title: Find the Right Abstraction

hybrid-certification.conclusion: 1. Use fast numerical computation (numpy, LAPACK, floating-point) to compute approximate answers: root locations, eigenvalues, sign patterns. 2. Design an exact verification step that checks the numerical answer: evaluate the polynomial at rational test points, verify sign conditions, count roots by IVT. 3. The exact step should be O(n) in the problem size (not O(n³) like the numerical step), since it's certifying known answers, not discovering them. 4. If the exact step disagrees with the numerical step, investigate rather than trust either.
hybrid-certification.however: The hybrid method must be provably correct. The numerical step identifies candidates; the exact step certifies them. If the certification step fails (e.g., the approximate root is too far from the true root for sign determination), the method must detect this and fall back rather than produce a wrong answer.
hybrid-certification.title: Hybrid Certification

induction-and-well-ordering.conclusion: Choose the right quantity to induct on. Verify the base case. For the inductive step, assume P holds for smaller values and show it holds for the current value. Consider strong induction if simple induction is too weak.
induction-and-well-ordering.however: The inductive step can be harder than it looks — it requires proving P(n+1) from P(n) (or from all P(k) with k<n for strong induction). Choosing the wrong induction variable makes the step impossible even when the theorem is true.
induction-and-well-ordering.title: Induction and Well-Ordering

local-to-global.conclusion: Cover the object with pieces where the property is manageable. Prove it on each piece. Check compatibility on overlaps. Glue the local results into a global one, using partitions of unity, sheaf conditions, or patching lemmas as appropriate.
local-to-global.however: Not every property is local. You must verify that local data can be patched: the pieces must be compatible on overlaps, and the patching procedure must not introduce new problems.
local-to-global.title: Local-to-Global Argument

monotone-approximation.conclusion: Construct a monotone sequence of simple objects converging to your target. Prove the result for each element of the sequence. Apply a monotone convergence or limit theorem to conclude for the general object.
monotone-approximation.however: Not all approximations are monotone, and not all properties survive limits. You must choose the right notion of approximation and verify that the limit argument is valid (monotone convergence theorem, continuity from below, directed completeness).
monotone-approximation.title: Monotone Approximation

numerical-scout.conclusion: 1. Grid evaluation: compute the function on a uniform grid over the domain. Record the minimum, maximum, and any near-zero values. 2. Critical point search: run multiple independent local optimization searches (L-BFGS, differential evolution) from random starting points. Use at least 3 independent searches with 1000+ starts each. 3. Domain boundary survey: evaluate on constraint boundaries (where disc=0, f=0, etc.). 4. Symmetry detection: check whether critical points cluster along symmetry subspaces. 5. Case structure identification: from the critical point map, identify natural subcases ordered by symmetry/difficulty.
numerical-scout.however: Numerical evidence does not constitute proof. Floating-point computation can miss critical points near boundaries, produce false precision, and confirm true conjectures whose proofs require entirely different techniques. The scout must inform the proof strategy, not replace it.
numerical-scout.title: Numerical Scout

optimise-a-free-parameter.conclusion: Differentiate (or otherwise optimise) with respect to the free parameter. If the optimum has a clean closed form, use it. If not, choose a value that balances the dominant terms — this typically gives the right order of magnitude.
optimise-a-free-parameter.however: The optimisation may be analytically intractable. In that case, a sub-optimal but explicit choice (often guided by dimensional analysis or balancing terms) is better than an opaque optimal one.
optimise-a-free-parameter.title: Optimise a Free Parameter

parametric-tension-dissolution.conclusion: 1. State the tension precisely: which obligations conflict on which parameter. 2. Ask: is there a different construction where both obligations want the same parameter value? This often means replacing the initial geometric or algebraic object (reflection → rotation, codim-1 → codim-2, etc.). 3. Check that the new construction still satisfies both obligations (it may make the previously-easy obligation slightly harder). 4. If the tension dissolves, record the resolution as a structural insight.
parametric-tension-dissolution.however: Not every difficulty is a tension. If obligation B merely "prefers" Y but can be completed with X, the tension is aesthetic, not structural. Only apply this pattern when the conflict genuinely blocks or severely impedes completion. Also: the alternative construction that dissolves the tension must exist — don't assume it does without checking.
parametric-tension-dissolution.title: Parametric Tension Dissolution

pass-to-a-subsequence.conclusion: Invoke compactness (Bolzano-Weierstrass, Alaoglu, Tychonoff, sequential compactness) to extract a convergent subsequence. Pass to it. Argue that the limit has the desired property. If necessary, show the limit is unique so the full sequence converges.
pass-to-a-subsequence.however: The subsequence may converge to something unwanted. You must verify that the limit has the properties you need, and that the argument does not depend on the specific subsequence chosen.
pass-to-a-subsequence.title: Pass to a Subsequence or Subnet

quotient-by-irrelevance.conclusion: Define an equivalence relation that identifies objects agreeing on what matters. Pass to the quotient. Verify well-definedness. Work in the quotient where the irrelevant distinctions are gone.
quotient-by-irrelevance.however: Quotienting loses information. You must verify that the operations and properties you care about are well-defined on equivalence classes, not just on representatives.
quotient-by-irrelevance.title: Quotient by Irrelevance

reduce-to-known-result.conclusion: Identify the candidate theorem. Compare its hypotheses to your situation. Bridge the gap: verify missing hypotheses, apply a change of variables, restrict to a subcase, or reformulate to match. Then invoke the theorem.
reduce-to-known-result.however: Forcing a reduction to the wrong theorem produces fragile, unenlightening proofs. The reduction step must be natural, not a contortion.
reduce-to-known-result.title: Reduce to a Known Result

separate-into-independent-pieces.conclusion: Arrange the construction so the pieces occupy disjoint regions (separated intervals, orthogonal subspaces, independent coordinates, disjoint cycles). Reduce the global quantity to a per-piece quantity using disjointness, then bound or compute piece by piece.
separate-into-independent-pieces.however: Independence must be *earned*, not assumed. You must verify the supports really are disjoint (or the events really are independent), and that disjointness actually delivers the aggregate property you need — e.g. that at most one piece is active at each point, so the aggregate reduces to a supremum/sum over single pieces with no cross-terms.
separate-into-independent-pieces.title: Separate into Independent Pieces

show-both-inequalities.conclusion: Prove A <= B and B <= A separately (or A is a subset of B and B is a subset of A). Combine to conclude A = B. For the squeeze/sandwich variant: bound A from above and below by quantities that both converge to the same limit.
show-both-inequalities.however: The two directions may require completely different techniques. One direction is often trivial while the other requires the bulk of the work. Identifying which is which saves effort.
show-both-inequalities.title: Show Both Inequalities

split-into-cases.conclusion: Identify the exhaustive partition. Prove the result separately for each case. Verify the cases are exhaustive (no gaps) and handle any overlap. Common splits: positive/ negative/zero, finite/infinite, convergent/divergent, trivial/non-trivial.
split-into-cases.however: Too many cases make a proof unreadable and suggest you are missing a unifying idea. If you find yourself with more than 3-4 cases, consider whether a different approach (symmetry, abstraction, contradiction) would eliminate the case split entirely.
split-into-cases.title: Split into Cases

structural-characterization.conclusion: 1. Identify the simpler components from which X can be built (Y plus a construction). 2. Establish the construction rigorously, with whatever uniqueness / universality clauses are appropriate. 3. Verify the structural identification by re-deriving known properties of X from the new description.
structural-characterization.however: Structural characterization differs from `find-the-right-abstraction` in direction: that pattern abstracts from many examples to a unifying framework; this pattern starts with one object and resolves it into simpler components. It also differs from `exhaustion-as-theorem`: that lists all instances of a type, this describes one instance fully. Choose this leaf when the deliverable is *one* full description, not a list.
structural-characterization.title: Structural Characterization

structural-equivalence.conclusion: 1. Construct both directions of the equivalence. 2. Verify they are mutually inverse (or mutually quasi-inverse, in the categorical case). 3. Verify preservation of the structural features of interest. 4. State the equivalence as a theorem; identify what consequences follow (since X and Y are structurally the same, anything proved about either is now available for both).
structural-equivalence.however: Structural equivalence is symmetric. It differs from `transport-across-isomorphism`: that pattern *uses* a known isomorphism to transfer a result; this pattern *establishes* a new structural identity. It also differs from `structural-inclusion`: that is directional; this is bidirectional. Use this leaf when the paper's contribution is a new equivalence.
structural-equivalence.title: Structural Equivalence

structural-inclusion.conclusion: 1. Identify the inclusion / embedding / domination map and verify it preserves the structural feature of interest. 2. Verify that the inclusion is strict (or note explicitly when it is tight / non-strict). 3. Identify the consequence: what holds for X because it holds for Y, or what fails to hold because the reverse inclusion does not.
structural-inclusion.however: Structural inclusion differs from `transport-across-isomorphism`: that pattern is symmetric (X ≅ Y); this pattern is directional (X ⊆ Y but not necessarily Y ⊆ X). Inclusion alone is weaker but often more useful in practice — many monotonicity results carry strict inclusion that no equivalence can replicate. Use this leaf when the relation is genuinely one-way.
structural-inclusion.title: Structural Inclusion / Monotonicity

structural-obstruction-as-theorem.conclusion: 1. State the obstruction precisely: what property of the problem blocks what method. 2. Prove the obstruction (even informally): show that the method CANNOT work, not just that it HASN'T worked. 3. Record the obstruction as a theorem or remark in the proof status document. 4. Use the obstruction to redirect: if method A is blocked, what does the obstruction tell you about which methods might succeed?
structural-obstruction-as-theorem.however: Not every failure is structural. Computational failures (memory, time, numerical instability) look like structural failures when resources are insufficient. Before claiming a structural obstruction, verify that increasing resources (degree, precision, time) does not help, or identify the algebraic reason for the failure.
structural-obstruction-as-theorem.title: Structural Obstruction as Theorem

technique-landscape-map.conclusion: 1. For each related method, construct a typed wiring diagram with nodes: Q (objective), D (decomposition), M (mechanism), C (certificate), O (output). 2. Add a bridge node B assessing the match to your target: direct, partial, or none. 3. For each B = partial, write down the exact structural mismatch. 4. Look for patterns across mismatches — they often share a common structural feature. 5. The common feature is the gap. Target it directly.
technique-landscape-map.however: Building the library is upfront investment that may feel premature. Not every problem needs it — only problems where the mismatch between existing methods and the target is non-obvious. If one method clearly applies modulo a minor adaptation, just adapt it.
technique-landscape-map.title: Technique Landscape Map

the-diagonal-argument.conclusion: Given the purported list f(1), f(2), ..., construct an object d that differs from f(n) at position n for every n. Since d differs from every listed item, d is not on the list, contradicting surjectivity.
the-diagonal-argument.however: The diagonal construction requires the ability to "flip" or modify the diagonal entry. Not all settings admit this. The argument also only gives non-existence; it does not say how much larger the target is.
the-diagonal-argument.title: The Diagonal Argument

transport-across-isomorphism.conclusion: Establish the isomorphism between X and Y. Prove the property for whichever side is easier. Invoke isomorphism-invariance to conclude for the other side. For structured settings, use the naturality of the isomorphism.
transport-across-isomorphism.however: You must verify that the property is indeed isomorphism-invariant. Not all properties transfer: a specific element, an embedding into a particular ambient space, or a computational representation may not survive transport.
transport-across-isomorphism.title: Transport Across an Isomorphism

try-a-simpler-case.conclusion: Reduce one or more parameters to the smallest non-trivial value. Solve that case. Examine what made it work and what would break if the parameter grew. Use the insight to guide the general argument.
try-a-simpler-case.however: Jumping to the simplest case can miss structure that only appears at intermediate complexity, and results for small cases do not always generalise.
try-a-simpler-case.title: Try a Simpler Case

unfold-the-definition.conclusion: Write out the definition of every technical term in the statement. Replace defined terms with their meanings. The proof obligation often becomes clear once the definitions are fully expanded. If multiple equivalent definitions exist, try each one.
unfold-the-definition.however: Definitions can unfold into multiple equivalent characterisations, and not all unfoldings are equally useful. Choosing the wrong characterisation can make the problem harder.
unfold-the-definition.title: Unfold the Definition

use-probabilistic-method.conclusion: Define a probability distribution on candidate objects. Show that the probability of having the desired property is positive (by union bound, expectation argument, Lovász local lemma, or second moment method). Conclude existence.
use-probabilistic-method.however: The probabilistic method typically does not produce an explicit object. It proves existence without construction. For applications requiring an actual witness, derandomisation techniques may be needed.
use-probabilistic-method.title: The Probabilistic Method

verify-universal-property.conclusion: State the universal property precisely. For existence: given an arbitrary test object and compatible data, construct the required morphism. For uniqueness: assume two morphisms work and show they are equal, typically by checking on generators or using a cancellation argument.
verify-universal-property.however: Universal properties require checking both existence and uniqueness of the mediating morphism. Existence is usually the construction; uniqueness is often the harder part and is where most proof errors occur.
verify-universal-property.title: Verify the Universal Property

work-examples-first.conclusion: Compute several concrete instances. Choose examples that are generic (not too symmetric), that test boundary conditions, and that span different regimes of the parameters. Record what each example teaches you about the conjecture.
work-examples-first.however: Examples alone do not prove theorems, and poorly chosen examples can mislead by being too special or too symmetric.
work-examples-first.title: Work Examples First
